explanations.explanation: Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet, walks in and finds the potter right in the middle of his work, "working at the wheel" (Jeremiah 18:3). No big temple, no crowd, just a man and some spinning clay. I think the LORD picked a spot where you could simply watch and learn. Sometimes the best classroom is somebody else's workshop.

No kiln shows up in this verse. Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet, finds the potter "working at the wheel," with the clay still being shaped (Jeremiah 18:3). Loading a kiln now would be like sliding a tray into the oven before the dough is even mixed. Wheel first, friend.

Nobody is buying anything in this scene. Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet, sees the potter "working at the wheel" (Jeremiah 18:3). The potter is busy making, not ringing up customers. I think that's the whole point of the visit: watch the hands.

That's exactly it. The verse says “…so he formed it into another vessel, as it seemed best for him to do.” (Jeremiah 18:4) The flaw doesn't end the clay's story. The potter just keeps going with the same lump and a new plan.

No trash can anywhere in this verse. The potter keeps the same clay in his hands, and “…he formed it into another vessel, as it seemed best for him to do.” (Jeremiah 18:4) A flawed vessel turned out to be a starting point. I've been tossed in a drawer before, so I'm glad this clay got a better deal.

The verse has no waiting around. The potter is still working it right there, and “…he formed it into another vessel, as it seemed best for him to do.” (Jeremiah 18:4) No pause, no walking away from the wheel. The flaw shows up and he's already on to the next shape.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, “Just like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel.” (Jeremiah 18:6) Israel is the clay, and the LORD is the potter holding it. That's the picture Jeremiah just watched at the wheel.

It's true, and the text says so plainly. The LORD asks, “…can I not treat you as this potter treats his clay?” and then says, “Just like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel.” (Jeremiah 18:6) The word comes right after Jeremiah watches the potter work. The wheel scene was the lesson.

It's the other way around. The LORD says, “But if that nation I warned turns from its evil, then I will relent of the disaster I had planned to bring.” (Jeremiah 18:8) A warning here is not a locked door. Turning around really does change what comes next.

Right, and here's what the text says: “But if that nation I warned turns from its evil, then I will relent of the disaster I had planned to bring.” (Jeremiah 18:8) The warning comes with a way out. When a nation turns, the disaster doesn't come as planned.

You've got it. The LORD says, “…then I will relent of the good I had intended for it.” (Jeremiah 18:10) This is the same teaching as before, just flipped. How a nation responds to Him matters, in both directions.

The verse says something different. When a nation does evil in His sight and doesn't listen to His voice, the LORD says, “…then I will relent of the good I had intended for it.” (Jeremiah 18:10) The good He intended doesn't just roll on regardless. It's a real answer to how the nation acts.

explanations.answer: He will pass it to another
explanations.explanation: No second nation shows up in this verse. The LORD only says, “…then I will relent of the good I had intended for it.” (Jeremiah 18:10) Nothing gets handed to anybody else. I can see why you'd guess it, but the text stops right at relenting.

That's the call. The LORD says, “Turn now, each of you, from your evil ways, and correct your ways and deeds.” (Jeremiah 18:11) Notice it's "each of you," so it's personal, not just a crowd move. The warning and the invitation come in the same breath.

Nobody is told to pack up in this verse. The LORD says, “Turn now, each of you, from your evil ways, and correct your ways and deeds.” (Jeremiah 18:11) The instruction is about ways and deeds, not about a change of address. Moving boxes won't fix this one, friend.

Offerings aren't mentioned here. The LORD says, “Turn now, each of you, from your evil ways, and correct your ways and deeds.” (Jeremiah 18:11) The call is to turn and fix how they live. You can't cover up a burnt batch by buying a fancier box.

It goes the opposite way. The LORD tells Jeremiah, “But they will reply, ‘It is hopeless. We will follow our own plans, and each of us will act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart.’” (Jeremiah 18:12) That's a flat no to the call to turn. No promise at all in that reply.

Right. The LORD says they will reply, “It is hopeless. We will follow our own plans, and each of us will act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart.” (Jeremiah 18:12) That's not a promise to turn, it's a refusal. After a call like the one in verse 11, that one stings.

That's the word. The LORD says, “Yet My people have forgotten Me.” (Jeremiah 18:15) Lebanon's snow and cool waters stay where they belong, and that makes the contrast hit. I think that's the point of the picture: some things you can count on, and His people didn't stay put like that.
The verse says the opposite. The LORD says, “Yet My people have forgotten Me.” (Jeremiah 18:15) They didn't follow Him. They burned incense to worthless idols instead.

Praise isn't what the verse says. The LORD says, “Yet My people have forgotten Me.” (Jeremiah 18:15) Right after that, the incense goes to worthless idols. The praise-shaped spot in their lives went to the wrong place.

explanations.answer: On rutted bypaths off the highway
explanations.explanation: That's what the LORD says: they're “leaving the ancient roads to walk on rutted bypaths instead of on the highway.” (Jeremiah 18:15) A rutted path is rough going the whole way. Think of rolling dough across a counter covered in crumbs. Nothing comes out smooth.

explanations.answer: On the ancient roads of old
explanations.explanation: They're leaving those roads, not walking them. The LORD says they're “leaving the ancient roads to walk on rutted bypaths instead of on the highway.” (Jeremiah 18:15) The old roads were right there and they stepped off. That's the whole complaint.

Egypt and the wilderness don't show up in this verse. The LORD says they're “leaving the ancient roads to walk on rutted bypaths instead of on the highway.” (Jeremiah 18:15) The picture is a rough back way beside the main road. It's an easy mix-up with other Bible journeys, but not this one.

Yes. The LORD says, “…all who pass by will be appalled and shake their heads.” (Jeremiah 18:16) The land itself will make people stop and stare. It's a whole row of head shakes from people who didn't even live there.

It's true. The LORD says the land will be a desolation and “…all who pass by will be appalled and shake their heads.” (Jeremiah 18:16) Even people just passing through will notice. It's a sad picture, friend.

explanations.answer: His back and not His face
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says, “I will show them My back and not My face in the day of their calamity.” (Jeremiah 18:17) I think this is one of the heavy parts of the chapter. It's a hard thing to read, so let's let it be hard.

The verse says the opposite. The LORD says, “I will show them My back and not My face in the day of their calamity.” (Jeremiah 18:17) No mercy is mentioned in that line. This is one of the heavy verses, and I won't dress it up.

No escape road appears here. The LORD says, “I will show them My back and not My face in the day of their calamity.” (Jeremiah 18:17) This is a heavy line, and the text just says it plainly. I think it's worth sitting quietly with it for a second.

explanations.answer: Denounce him and ignore his words
explanations.explanation: That's their plan. Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet, hears them say, “Come, let us denounce him and pay no heed to any of his words.” (Jeremiah 18:18) It's like muting a group chat so you never have to read what's in it. They're sure they'll be fine without his message.

explanations.answer: Bring his words to the king
explanations.explanation: No king appears in this verse. Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet, is up against people who say, “Come, let us denounce him and pay no heed to any of his words.” (Jeremiah 18:18) Taking his words to anyone would mean listening to them. Their plan is to do the opposite.

explanations.answer: Write his words on a scroll
explanations.explanation: Nobody grabs a scroll here. Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet, hears them say, “Come, let us denounce him and pay no heed to any of his words.” (Jeremiah 18:18) Writing it down would be keeping it. They want to pay it no heed.
That's the word. Jeremiah asks, “Should good be repaid with evil?” (Jeremiah 18:20) I think that one hurts. It's the question of someone who tried to help and got a trap in return.

Thanks is what you'd hope for, and that's what makes the question sting. Jeremiah asks, “Should good be repaid with evil?” (Jeremiah 18:20) Evil is the word in the verse. I think the pain in that question is the gap between what he gave and what he got.
Silence isn't the word here. Jeremiah asks, “Should good be repaid with evil?” (Jeremiah 18:20) It's a harder word than silence. I think this is a man hurting and saying so out loud to the LORD.

Yes. Jeremiah tells the LORD, “Remember how I stood before You to speak good on their behalf, to turn Your wrath from them.” (Jeremiah 18:20) He stood in front of the LORD for the very people now plotting against him. No wonder he's asking if good gets repaid with evil.

No hiding in this verse. Jeremiah tells the LORD, “Remember how I stood before You to speak good on their behalf, to turn Your wrath from them.” (Jeremiah 18:20) What he did was speak up for them. It's a lot like standing next to someone in a meeting and saying a kind word when they weren't even in the room.

Money doesn't come up in this verse. Jeremiah tells the LORD, “Remember how I stood before You to speak good on their behalf, to turn Your wrath from them.” (Jeremiah 18:20) What he gave them was his voice, standing before the LORD. That's a costly thing to give.
Yes. Jeremiah says, “…for they have dug a pit to capture me and have hidden snares for my feet.” (Jeremiah 18:22) That's a pit and snares both. I think he's laying the whole picture out for the LORD.

It's true. Jeremiah says, “…for they have dug a pit to capture me and have hidden snares for my feet.” (Jeremiah 18:22) The pit and the snares are both in his words. I think he wants the LORD to see every piece of it.

It's the opposite. Jeremiah prays, “Do not wipe out their guilt or blot out their sin from Your sight.” (Jeremiah 18:23) This is a heavy prayer, and the text doesn't soften it. He asks the LORD to leave their guilt where it is.

Right. Jeremiah prays, “Do not wipe out their guilt or blot out their sin from Your sight.” (Jeremiah 18:23) That's the reverse of asking for it to be wiped out. It's a heavy prayer, and I think it shows how much he's hurting.
